Tielman Susato.fact: A trumpet player and music publisher in Antwerp. He printed lots of dance music, including the Ronde in our book.

Johann Schop.fact: A violinist who worked in Hamburg. Bach later used Schop's melody in “Jesu, Joy of Man's Desiring.”

Jeremiah Clarke.fact: For many years his Trumpet Voluntary was printed under another composer's name: Henry Purcell.

Johann Sebastian Bach.fact: Bach's death in 1750 marks the end of the Baroque Period.

George Frideric Handel.fact: Born in Germany, famous in England. His Water Music was played on a barge on the Thames River for King George I (1717).

Jean-Jacques Rousseau.fact: Better known as a philosopher. A dance from his 1752 opera became the tune of “Go Tell Aunt Rhodie.”

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart.fact: A child prodigy: he toured Europe with his father, wrote his first symphony at 8 and his first opera at 12.

Ludwig van Beethoven.fact: He was completely deaf when he wrote Symphony No. 9 (1824). His music bridges the Classical and Romantic Periods.

Jacques Offenbach.fact: Born in Germany, he became a star in Paris. He was also a fine cellist.

J. S. Pierpont.fact: He was music director at the Unitarian church right here in Savannah when “Jingle Bells” was published in 1857.

Stephen Foster.fact: America's first great popular songwriter, born on July 4, 1826: the 50th birthday of American independence.

Peter Ilyich Tchaikovsky.fact: He studied to be a lawyer first. In 1891 he traveled to New York City for the opening of Carnegie Hall.

John Philip Sousa.fact: “The March King.” He led the U.S. Marine Band, and the sousaphone is named after him.

Gustav Holst.fact: He was a professional trombonist. His most famous piece is The Planets.

Percy Grainger.fact: Born in Australia, he collected English folk songs and later lived in the United States. His band pieces are band classics.

Bruce Pearson.fact: Played clarinet and saxophone (and baseball and hockey!) in college before becoming a music teacher, author, composer and conductor.

Anne McGinty.fact: One of the most prolific women composers of band music: more than 225 published pieces.

Erin A. Watson.fact: Plays violin, piano and accordion, and studied with American composer Joan Tower.

Ryan Nowlin.fact: A composer, author and music teacher who also plays horn and sings. He co-wrote this book.

songs.title: Hot Cross Buns
songs.label: English Folk Song
songs.fact: Once a street vendors' call for selling buns in England.

songs.title: Go Tell Aunt Rhodie
songs.label: American Folk Song
songs.fact: The tune is older than the song: it began as a dance in Rousseau's 1752 opera in France.

songs.title: Merrily We Roll Along
songs.label: Traditional (American)
songs.fact: Same tune as “Mary Had a Little Lamb.”

songs.title: Good King Wenceslas
songs.label: Traditional English Carol
songs.fact: English words (1853), a tune from a 1582 songbook printed for Finland, and a real duke of Bohemia (today's Czechia).

also.why: Wenceslas was a real duke of Bohemia (today's Czechia) in the 900s

songs.title: The Frog's Song
songs.label: Japanese Folk Song
songs.fact: In Japan it's called “Kaeru no Uta” and is sung as a round.

songs.title: Russian Folk Song
songs.label: Ludwig van Beethoven (a Russian folk tune)

songs.title: Jingle Bells
songs.label: J. S. Pierpont
songs.fact: Savannah has a historical marker for it! The sleigh rides in the song are from Massachusetts, where Pierpont grew up. It was also the first song ever played in space (Gemini 6, 1965).

also.why: Pierpont grew up here; the song was published in Boston in 1857

songs.title: The Dreidel Song
songs.label: Jewish Folk Song
songs.fact: The English song “I Have a Little Dreidel” was written by Samuel Goldfarb in New York in the 1920s. A dreidel is a spinning top for Hanukkah.

songs.title: Now Let Me Fly
songs.label: American Spiritual
songs.fact: Spirituals are religious folk songs created by enslaved African Americans in the 1700s and 1800s.

songs.title: Carnival of Venice
songs.label: Italian Folk Song
songs.fact: Venice's Carnival is famous for its masks. Many virtuosos have written show-off variations on this tune.

songs.title: Streets of Laredo
songs.label: American Folk Song
songs.fact: Laredo is a city in Texas on the Mexican border. It's a cowboy song.

songs.title: Theme from “The Nutcracker”
songs.label: Peter Ilyich Tchaikovsky
songs.fact: The Nutcracker ballet first played in St. Petersburg in 1892. Now theaters everywhere perform it every December.

songs.title: Procession from “Water Music”
songs.label: George Frideric Handel
songs.fact: Written for a royal boat party on the Thames River. The orchestra played on one barge while King George I listened from another.

songs.title: Banana Boat Song
songs.label: Jamaican Folk Song
songs.fact: A work song sung by dock workers loading bananas onto ships at night, made world-famous by Harry Belafonte in 1956.

songs.title: Fais Dodo
songs.label: French Folk Song
songs.fact: “Fais dodo” is how French parents say “go to sleep” to little kids.

songs.title: La Bamba
songs.label: Mexican Folk Song
songs.fact: A wedding song from Veracruz, Mexico. Ritchie Valens made a rock-and-roll version a hit in 1958.

songs.title: Theme from “Orpheus in the Underworld”
songs.label: Jacques Offenbach
songs.fact: Its fastest section is the famous “can-can” dance music.

songs.title: Santa Lucia
songs.label: Italian Folk Song
songs.fact: A boat song about a harbor in Naples. In Sweden, it's sung on St. Lucia's Day every December 13.

songs.title: When the Saints Go Marching In
songs.label: American Spiritual
songs.fact: Often played in Dixieland jazz style, which began in New Orleans in the early 1900s.

songs.title: Alouette
songs.label: French Canadian Folk Song
songs.fact: “Alouette” means “lark,” a kind of songbird.

songs.title: Trumpet Voluntary
songs.label: Jeremiah Clarke
songs.fact: Also called “Prince of Denmark's March.” It was first written for harpsichord, and it's a favorite at weddings.

songs.title: Theme from “Symphony No. 9”
songs.label: Ludwig van Beethoven
songs.fact: Called “Ode to Joy.” Beethoven was completely deaf when he wrote it, and it first played in Vienna in 1824.

songs.title: Lone Star Waltz
songs.label: Erin A. Watson
songs.fact: Texas is called the Lone Star State.

songs.title: Yangtze Boatman Chantey
songs.label: Chinese Folk Song
songs.fact: The Yangtze is the longest river in Asia.

songs.title: Mary Ann
songs.label: Calypso Song
songs.fact: Calypso began in Trinidad and Tobago in the early 1900s. It often features guitar, steel drums and other percussion.

songs.title: Amazing Grace
songs.label: American Folk Song
songs.fact: The words were written by John Newton, an English minister, in the 1770s. The tune we sing (“New Britain”) is American.

also.why: John Newton wrote the words here

songs.title: A Little Blue
songs.label: In the style of the blues
songs.fact: The blues grew out of African American spirituals and work songs in the early 1900s. Blues melodies are usually 12 measures long.

songs.title: Samba-lêlê
songs.label: Brazilian Folk Song
songs.fact: A children's song from Brazil, where samba is the sound of Carnival.

songs.title: Ye Banks and Braes o' Bonnie Doon
songs.label: Scottish Folk Song
songs.fact: The words are by Robert Burns, Scotland's national poet. The Doon is a river in Ayrshire.

songs.title: Shepherd's Hey
songs.label: English Folk Song
songs.fact: Percy Grainger's 1918 version for concert band is part of the band world's standard music.

songs.title: Manhattan Beach March
songs.label: John Philip Sousa
songs.fact: Named for a seaside resort in Brooklyn, New York, where Sousa's band played summer concerts.

songs.title: Ecossaise for Military Band
songs.label: Ludwig van Beethoven
songs.fact: Written in 1810. An écossaise is a lively dance; “military band” was an old name for a band like ours.

songs.title: See, the Conquering Hero Comes
songs.label: George Frideric Handel
songs.fact: From Judas Maccabaeus (1746), one of Handel's most famous oratorios.

songs.title: German Dance
songs.label: Ludwig van Beethoven
songs.fact: Written around 1795, when Beethoven was becoming famous in Vienna as a composer and pianist.

United States of America.known: Jazz, rock and roll, national parks and marching bands
United States of America.fact: The tune of “The Star-Spangled Banner” was a British song before Francis Scott Key wrote new words in 1814.
United States of America.music: Jazz was born in New Orleans in the early 1900s, and the blues grew up in the South.

United Kingdom.known: Big Ben, castles, the Beatles and tea
United Kingdom.fact: The UK is four countries in one: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
United Kingdom.music: The Beatles came from Liverpool, England. Scotland is famous for bagpipes.

Ireland.known: Green hills, St. Patrick's Day and Irish dance
Ireland.fact: The harp is Ireland's national symbol. It's even on Irish coins.
Ireland.music: Irish folk bands use the fiddle, tin whistle and a frame drum called the bodhrán.

Germany.known: Castles, pretzels, the Black Forest and fast cars
Germany.fact: Johannes Gutenberg's printing press, made in Mainz around 1450, changed how the world shared books and music.
Germany.music: Bach, Handel and Beethoven were all born in Germany. So were the clarinet and the tuba.

Austria.known: The Alps, skiing and Vienna's music
Austria.fact: Vienna is called the “City of Music”: Mozart, Haydn and Beethoven all worked there.
Austria.music: The waltz became the dance craze of Vienna. Johann Strauss II wrote “The Blue Danube.”

France.known: The Eiffel Tower, art museums and croissants
France.fact: The Eiffel Tower was built for a world's fair in 1889 and was supposed to be temporary.
France.music: The oboe was developed at the French royal court in the 1600s.

Italy.known: Pizza, pasta, Rome and the Leaning Tower of Pisa
Italy.fact: Most of our music words are Italian: piano, forte, allegro, crescendo, tempo…
Italy.music: The piano was invented in Florence, Italy, around 1700.

Spain.fact: Flamenco dancers and singers clap tricky rhythms called palmas.
Spain.music: The modern classical guitar was developed in Spain in the 1800s.

Russia.known: The world's biggest country, ballet and snowy winters
Russia.music: Tchaikovsky's ballets, like The Nutcracker, are performed all over the world.

Japan.known: Sushi, anime, video games and bullet trains
Japan.fact: Japan's bullet trains (Shinkansen) travel close to 200 miles per hour.
Japan.music: Taiko drummers play huge drums using their whole bodies.

China.known: The Great Wall, giant pandas and Lunar New Year
China.fact: Paper and the compass were first invented in China.
China.music: The erhu is a two-string Chinese fiddle played with a bow.

Mexico.known: Tacos, ancient pyramids and Day of the Dead
Mexico.fact: The Aztecs and Maya were drinking chocolate long before Europeans arrived.
Mexico.music: Mariachi bands play trumpets, violins and several sizes of guitar.

Puerto Rico.known: Beaches, the El Morro fortress and the coquí frog
Puerto Rico.fact: Puerto Rico is a U.S. territory, so people born there are U.S. citizens.
Puerto Rico.music: Bomba and plena are Puerto Rican music styles built on drums and call-and-response singing.

Jamaica.fact: Usain Bolt, the fastest sprinter ever timed, is from Jamaica.
Jamaica.music: Reggae music, made famous by Bob Marley, comes from Jamaica.

Trinidad and Tobago.fact: The first steel pans were made from old oil drums.
Trinidad and Tobago.music: Calypso and soca music both come from Trinidad and Tobago.

Canada.fact: Canada has the longest coastline of any country in the world.
Canada.music: In Quebec most people speak French. Songs like “Alouette” come from there.

Australia.known: Kangaroos, koalas and the Sydney Opera House
Australia.fact: Australia is a country and a whole continent.
Australia.music: The didgeridoo is an ancient wind instrument of Aboriginal Australians.

Sweden.known: ABBA, IKEA and the Northern Lights
Sweden.fact: Sweden has an Ice Hotel that is rebuilt from river ice every winter.
Sweden.music: ABBA, one of the best-selling bands of all time, is from Sweden.

Brazil.known: Soccer, the Amazon rainforest and Carnival
Brazil.fact: Most of the Amazon rainforest is in Brazil.
Brazil.music: Samba drums power Brazil's giant Carnival parades.

South Africa.known: Safaris, Table Mountain and Nelson Mandela
South Africa.music: South African choirs are famous for rich harmony singing.

Belgium.fact: Adolphe Sax, the inventor of the saxophone, was born in Dinant, Belgium.
Belgium.music: In the 1500s, Antwerp was a center for printing music.

Finland.fact: Finland is sometimes called the “Land of a Thousand Lakes,” but it really has far more.
Finland.music: The tune of “Good King Wenceslas” was printed in Piae Cantiones, a 1582 songbook for Finland.

Czechia.fact: Good King Wenceslas was a real duke of Bohemia (today's Czechia) more than 1,000 years ago.
Czechia.music: Antonín Dvořák was Czech. He wrote his “New World” Symphony while living in America.

Switzerland.fact: Switzerland has four official languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh.
Switzerland.music: The alphorn is a long wooden horn once used to call across mountain valleys.

Guatemala.fact: Tikal, an ancient Maya city, rises out of Guatemala's rainforest.
Guatemala.music: The marimba is Guatemala's national instrument.

Turkey.fact: Istanbul is a city on two continents, Europe and Asia.
Turkey.music: The Zildjian cymbal company started in Istanbul in 1623 and still makes cymbals today.

Cuba.known: Old classic cars and Caribbean beaches
Cuba.fact: Cuba is the largest island in the Caribbean.
Cuba.music: Cuban son music, a mix of Spanish and African sounds, helped give the world salsa.

Argentina.known: Tango, soccer and the Andes mountains
Argentina.fact: Aconcagua in Argentina is the tallest mountain in the world outside Asia.
Argentina.music: The tango was born in Buenos Aires.

Indonesia.known: Thousands of islands and Komodo dragons
Indonesia.music: Gamelan orchestras play gongs and metal xylophones together.

India.known: The Taj Mahal, cricket and spicy food
India.fact: India has more people than any other country.
India.music: The sitar has many extra strings that ring along on their own when other strings are played.

Egypt.known: The pyramids and the Nile River
Egypt.fact: The Great Pyramid was the tallest building on Earth for about 3,800 years.
Egypt.music: Ancient Egyptians played harps, flutes and a rattle called a sistrum.

Kenya.fact: Kenyan runners have won many Olympic medals in long-distance races.

Ghana.fact: In 1957 Ghana became the first country south of the Sahara to win independence from colonial rule.
Ghana.music: Talking drums can copy the rise and fall of spoken words.

Mali.fact: Timbuktu was once a great center of learning with huge libraries of handwritten books.
Mali.music: Griots are storytelling musicians. Many play the kora, a 21-string harp.

New Zealand.known: Mountains, kiwi birds and the Māori haka
New Zealand.fact: There are more sheep than people in New Zealand.
New Zealand.music: The haka is a Māori dance with chanting, stamping and strong voices.

Norway.known: Fjords, Vikings and the midnight sun
Norway.fact: In northern Norway the sun doesn't set at all for weeks in summer.
Norway.music: Edvard Grieg, from Norway, wrote “In the Hall of the Mountain King.”

Netherlands.fact: About a quarter of the Netherlands is below sea level.

Portugal.fact: Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese explorer, led the first voyage around the world (his crew finished it).
Portugal.music: Fado is a soulful song style from Lisbon.

Greece.fact: The Olympic Games began in ancient Greece about 2,800 years ago.
Greece.music: The word “music” comes from the Muses, the Greek goddesses of the arts.

Poland.known: Pierogi and the old city of Kraków
Poland.fact: Marie Curie, the first person to win two Nobel Prizes, was born in Warsaw.
Poland.music: Composer and pianist Frédéric Chopin was born in Poland.

Hungary.fact: The Rubik's Cube was invented in Hungary in 1974.
Hungary.music: Composer Béla Bartók traveled to villages to record Hungarian folk songs.

South Korea.fact: Korea's alphabet, Hangul, was created in the 1440s.
South Korea.music: K-pop groups are known for their tightly practiced dance routines.

Peru.fact: Machu Picchu is an Inca city built high in the Andes mountains in the 1400s.
Peru.music: Andean bands play panpipes and the charango, a small guitar.

Mongolia.known: Horses, yurts and the Gobi Desert
Mongolia.fact: Mongolia has more horses than people.
Mongolia.music: Mongolian throat singers can sing two notes at the same time.

Nepal.known: Mount Everest, the world's tallest mountain
Nepal.fact: Nepal's flag is the only national flag that isn't a rectangle.

Madagascar.fact: Lemurs live in the wild only on Madagascar.
Madagascar.music: The valiha is a tube-shaped string instrument made from bamboo.

Venezuela.fact: Angel Falls is the world's tallest waterfall.
Venezuela.music: El Sistema, a free youth orchestra program that inspired programs around the world, started in Venezuela in 1975.

Colombia.fact: Colombia has coasts on both the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea.
Colombia.music: Cumbia music began on Colombia's Caribbean coast.

Philippines.fact: The Philippines has more than 7,000 islands.

Thailand.fact: Thailand is the only country in Southeast Asia that was never ruled by a European power.

Vietnam.known: Ha Long Bay and rice paddies
Vietnam.fact: Ha Long Bay has about 1,600 limestone islands.
Vietnam.music: The đàn bầu has just one string. Players bend its pitch with a flexible rod.

Nigeria.fact: Nigeria has the most people of any country in Africa.
Nigeria.music: Afrobeat music was created by Nigerian musician Fela Kuti.

Morocco.known: Markets, deserts and the Atlas Mountains
Morocco.fact: The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, founded in 859, is often called the oldest university still open.
Morocco.music: Gnawa musicians play the guembri, a three-string bass lute.

Ethiopia.known: Coffee and ancient churches carved from rock
Ethiopia.fact: Coffee plants first grew wild in Ethiopia.

Chile.known: The Andes and Easter Island's giant statues
Chile.fact: The Atacama Desert in Chile is one of the driest places on Earth.

Ukraine.fact: Ukraine is the largest country entirely in Europe.
Ukraine.music: The melody of “Carol of the Bells” comes from a Ukrainian folk chant called “Shchedryk.”

Tanzania.fact: Mount Kilimanjaro is the tallest mountain in Africa.

instruments.name: Flute
instruments.fact: Theobald Böhm designed the modern metal flute in Munich. Flutes carved from bird and mammoth bones, found in German caves, are more than 35,000 years old.

instruments.name: Oboe
instruments.fact: The oboe was developed by musicians at the French royal court. Its name comes from the French “hautbois”: high wood.

instruments.name: Clarinet
instruments.fact: Johann Christoph Denner of Nuremberg improved an older instrument called the chalumeau and created the clarinet.

instruments.name: Bassoon
instruments.fact: The bassoon grew out of the dulcian of the 1500s. The Heckel family workshop in Biebrich, Germany, shaped the bassoon most players use today.

instruments.name: Saxophone
instruments.fact: Adolphe Sax was born in Dinant, Belgium, and patented the saxophone in Paris in 1846. He wanted an instrument with the power of brass and the agility of woodwinds.

instruments.name: Trumpet (valves)
instruments.fact: Valves were patented in 1818 by Heinrich Stölzel and Friedrich Blühmel in Prussia (Germany). Before valves, trumpets could play only a few notes.

instruments.name: French Horn
instruments.fact: Hunting horns were popular in France, but the valve horn we play was developed in Germany. In many countries it's just called “horn.”

instruments.name: Trombone
instruments.fact: The trombone began as the sackbut. Nuremberg's brass makers were famous for them in the 1500s, and the slide works the same way today.

instruments.name: Euphonium & Tuba
instruments.fact: Wilhelm Wieprecht and Johann Moritz patented the bass tuba in Berlin in 1835. The euphonium followed in Germany in the 1840s.

instruments.name: Cymbals
instruments.fact: The Zildjian family began making cymbals in Istanbul in 1623 using a secret metal recipe. The company still makes cymbals today, now in Massachusetts.

instruments.name: Timpani
instruments.fact: Kettledrums came to Europe from the Middle East, often played on horseback with trumpets.

instruments.name: Marimba
instruments.fact: The marimba has African roots and became Guatemala's national instrument.

instruments.name: Piano
instruments.fact: Bartolomeo Cristofori invented the piano in Florence. Its full name, pianoforte, means it can play soft and loud.

instruments.name: Steel Pan
instruments.fact: Invented in Trinidad and Tobago from oil drums. Pan players tune each note by hammering the metal.
